lead: One equilibrium stage leaves part of the solute in the raffinate. In cross-current extraction the raffinate from one stage is contacted again with a fresh portion of solvent, stage after stage, and each extract is drawn off separately. When the carrier and solvent are immiscible and the distribution ratio is constant, every stage removes the same fraction of what is left, so the solute falls geometrically and one formula gives the result. Cross-current contact is the arithmetic of batch extraction in a laboratory funnel and of small multi-product plants; large continuous plants use counter-current flow, the next chapter.
prereq: You need Liquid-liquid extraction and ternary diagrams (lever rule, solute-free ratios X and Y).

blocks.text: Take B and S as immiscible. Then the carrier flow B (kg) leaves entirely in the raffinate and the solvent S (kg) entirely in the extract, and the solute is followed with ratios: X = kg A per kg B, Y = kg A per kg S. Equilibrium is Y = K′X, where K′ is the distribution ratio on this basis (it differs from the mass-fraction K).
A solute balance on one ideal stage fed with pure solvent: B X<sub>0</sub> = B X<sub>1</sub> + S Y<sub>1</sub>, with Y<sub>1</sub> = K′X<sub>1</sub>. Solving gives the result below.

blocks.where: X<sub>0</sub> and X<sub>1</sub> are kg solute per kg carrier in the feed and the raffinate; S is kg of pure solvent; B is kg of carrier; ε is the extraction factor, the solute leaving in the extract divided by the solute left in the raffinate for one ideal stage (dimensionless).

blocks.text: On a triangular diagram, when B and S partly dissolve each other, the same stage is drawn: join F to S, locate M by the lever rule (FM/MS = S/F), draw the tie line through M (by interpolation between measured tie lines), and read E<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>1</sub> at its ends.

In stage n the raffinate R<sub>n−1</sub> meets a fresh solvent portion S<sub>n</sub>, and the extract E<sub>n</sub> is withdrawn. With equal portions and constant K′, every stage has the same ε and the same balance repeats.

blocks.where: X<sub>n</sub> is the raffinate ratio after n ideal stages, each fed S kg of pure solvent. Fraction recovered = 1 − 1/(1 + ε)<sup>n</sup>; fraction left in the raffinate = 1/(1 + ε)<sup>n</sup>.

items: Graphically on the triangle, stage 1 is drawn as above.

R<sub>1</sub> becomes the feed of stage 2: join R<sub>1</sub> to S, place M<sub>2</sub> with R<sub>1</sub>M<sub>2</sub>/M<sub>2</sub>S = S<sub>2</sub>/R<sub>1</sub>, and draw the tie line through M<sub>2</sub>.
Repeat until the raffinate composition reaches the target; the number of tie lines drawn is the number of ideal stages.

On an X–Y plot (immiscible case) each stage is a straight line of slope −B/S<sub>n</sub> from (X<sub>n−1</sub>, 0) to the equilibrium curve; where it meets the curve is (X<sub>n</sub>, Y<sub>n</sub>).

blocks.text: For a fixed total solvent and constant K′, equal portions leave the least solute: the product of the (1 + ε<sub>n</sub>) terms is largest when the portions are equal. More stages always help, but with diminishing return. With a total solvent S<sub>T</sub> split into very many portions, X<sub>n</sub>/X<sub>0</sub> approaches e<sup>−K′S<sub>T</sub>/B</sup>, a limit that no number of cross-current stages can pass.

A real stage that is mixed for too short a time does not reach equilibrium. The stage efficiency η is the actual fall in raffinate ratio divided by the fall in an ideal stage: η = (X<sub>n−1</sub> − X<sub>n</sub>)/(X<sub>n−1</sub> − X<sub>n</sub>*), where X<sub>n</sub>* = X<sub>n−1</sub>/(1 + ε) is the ideal value. Rearranged, each real stage leaves X<sub>n</sub> = X<sub>n−1</sub>[1 − η ε/(1 + ε)].

The overall efficiency is the number of ideal stages divided by the number of real stages needed for the same duty. Keep the two apart: a stage efficiency of 0.7 does not mean that 3 real stages equal 2.1 ideal ones; the worked example shows how to count them.

examples.question: 500 kg of a solution containing 125 kg solute and 375 kg carrier is extracted in three ideal cross-current stages, each with 200 kg of pure solvent. Carrier and solvent are immiscible and Y = 2.0X (both kg solute per kg solute-free liquid). Find the solute left and the recovery. Compare with putting all 600 kg of solvent into one stage.
steps: Extraction factor per stage: ε = K′S/B = 2.0 × 200/375 = 1.0667; 1 + ε = 2.0667.
Solute left = 0.03776 × 375 = 14.16 kg; recovered = 125 − 14.16 = 110.84 kg, that is 88.7 %.
Extract loadings: Y<sub>1</sub> = 2 × 0.1613 = 0.3226, Y<sub>2</sub> = 0.1560, Y<sub>3</sub> = 0.0755 kg/kg, so the three extracts carry 64.5, 31.2 and 15.1 kg (sum 110.8 kg).
One stage with 600 kg: ε = 2.0 × 600/375 = 3.2, X<sub>1</sub> = 0.3333/4.2 = 0.0794; solute left 29.76 kg, recovery 76.2 %.
examples.answer: Three stages of 200 kg leave 14.16 kg (88.7 % recovered); one stage of 600 kg leaves 29.76 kg (76.2 %). The extracts get leaner stage by stage, from 0.323 to 0.076 kg/kg.

examples.question: The same stages run at a stage efficiency η = 0.7. Find the recovery in three real stages and the number of real stages needed to match the 14.16 kg of the three ideal stages.
steps: Fraction removed by one ideal stage: ε/(1 + ε) = 1.0667/2.0667 = 0.5161.
One real stage keeps 1 − 0.7 × 0.5161 = 0.6387 of the solute entering it.
Three real stages: 0.6387³ = 0.2606, so 0.2606 × 125 = 32.6 kg is left and the recovery is 73.9 %.
Target: 14.16/125 = 0.1133 left. Real stages n = ln 0.1133/ln 0.6387 = (−2.178)/(−0.4483) = 4.86, so 5 real stages are needed.
examples.answer: Three real stages recover 73.9 %; 5 real stages are needed to do the work of 3 ideal ones (overall efficiency 3/5 = 0.6).

traps: Recovery after n stages is 1 − 1/(1 + ε)<sup>n</sup>, not n times the one-stage recovery; three stages of 51.6 % each give 88.7 %, not 155 %.
B in ε = K′S/B is the carrier alone (375 kg), not the feed (500 kg).
K′ on ratios and K on mass fractions are different numbers; use the one the question gives, or convert with X = x/(1 − x).
Unequal portions (400, 100, 100 kg) give 1 + ε of 3.133, 1.533, 1.533 with product 7.37 against 8.83 for equal portions, so they leave more solute: 17.0 kg against 14.2 kg.
Stage efficiency 0.7 does not turn 3 real stages into 2.1 ideal ones; count the stages from the real-stage factor.

quiz.q: Define the extraction factor ε for one cross-current stage.
quiz.a: ε = K′S/B: the distribution ratio times the solvent per stage divided by the carrier. It is the ratio of solute leaving in the extract to solute left in the raffinate for one ideal stage.

quiz.q: Why do three portions of 200 kg remove more solute than one of 600 kg?
quiz.a: Each stage removes the fraction ε/(1 + ε) of what is left, and the fractions multiply: three stages leave 1/2.0667³ = 0.113, one big stage leaves 1/4.2 = 0.238. In a single stage the whole solvent ends at the same lean extract loading; split up, the early portions leave rich and the late ones still find solute to take.

quiz.q: X<sub>0</sub> = 0.4 kg/kg, K′ = 1.5, S/B = 1.0 per stage. Find X after two ideal cross-current stages.
400 kg of a 20 mass% solution is washed twice with 150 kg of pure solvent each time; K′ = 3.0 on ratios. Find the solute left and the recovery.
How is the mixture point of the second stage located on a triangular diagram?
quiz.a: Join R<sub>1</sub> (raffinate of stage 1) to the solvent point S and place M<sub>2</sub> on that line so that R<sub>1</sub>M<sub>2</sub>/M<sub>2</sub>S = S<sub>2</sub>/R<sub>1</sub>; the tie line through M<sub>2</sub> gives E<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>2</sub>.

quiz.q: With 600 kg of solvent for the feed of the worked example, what is the best recovery cross-current flow can ever give?
quiz.a: With very many equal portions X<sub>n</sub>/X<sub>0</sub> → e<sup>−K′S<sub>T</sub>/B</sup> = e<sup>−2 × 600/375</sup> = e<sup>−3.2</sup> = 0.041, so at most 95.9 % is recovered however many stages are used. Three stages already give 88.7 %; the rest costs many more stages.

quiz.q: Distinguish stage efficiency from overall efficiency.
quiz.a: Stage efficiency is the actual change in one stage divided by the ideal change. Overall efficiency is ideal stages divided by real stages for the whole duty.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large plants seldom use cross-current trains because the solvent use is high and the combined extract is dilute; counter-current batteries dominate. The cross-current recursion still governs laboratory separatory-funnel work, multiple washing of filter cakes and many small pharmaceutical batches. The same recursion with the stripping factor appears in tray absorbers, and its counter-current version is the Kremser equation. Search for multiple-contact batch extraction and the Kremser equation.
